slides.title: Good, better, best
slides.text:
**good**: one thing
**better**: compare two things
**best**: compare three or more

My kite is good. Your kite is **better**. Omar's kite is the **best**.

slides.title: No -er here
slides.text:
We never say gooder or goodest.

✓ better
✓ best

slides.title: Use than
slides.text:
With **better**, we often use **than**.

My kite is **better than** yours.

With **best**, we often use **the**: the **best** kite.

proof.title: Prove it from the text
proof.text:
1. Find the blank.
2. Count: how many things are compared?
3. Look for clue words: **than** (two), **of all** (many).

Point to the clue words.

sentences.t: Hind's drawing is the best of all.

example.explain:
Sara's drawing is compared with Ali's: two drawings → **better**.

Hind's is compared with all of them → **the best**.

together.passage: Three friends made juice. Nora's juice was good. Lama's juice was better. Reem's juice was the ___ of all.
together.hint: How many juices are compared? Look at the words of all.
together.good: Yes! Three juices are compared, so Reem's is the best of all.

sentences: Three friends made juice.
Nora's juice was good.
Lama's juice was better.
Reem's juice was the ___ of all.
evidence.stem: The answer was: best. Tap 2 sentences that show three or more things are compared.
evidence.wrong: This sentence tells about one or two juices. Find the clues that show three or more.

checks.passage: My new bike is ___ than my old bike.
checks.why: Two bikes are compared, and the sentence has than, so we use better.

checks.passage: This is the ___ day of my life!
checks.why: This day is compared with all the days of my life, so it is the best.

checks.passage: Rami's sandwich is gooder than mine.
checks.why: Gooder is not a word. Two sandwiches are compared, so we use better.

again.title: Count them
again.text:
Count how many things you compare.

**One** → good
**Two** → better
**Three or more** → best
again.example:
Apples are good. Mangoes are better. Dates are the best!

Dates are compared with **all** the fruits, so they are the **best**.

slides.title: Bad, worse, worst
slides.text:
**bad**: one thing
**worse**: compare two
**worst**: compare three or more

Never say badder or baddest.

slides.title: Two or more?
slides.text:
Comparing **two** → better or worse, often with **than**.

Comparing **three or more** → **the** best or **the** worst.

slides.title: Clue words
slides.text:
**than** → better, worse

**the ... of all**, **in the class**, **ever** → best, worst

Clue words tell you which form to use.

proof.title: Prove it from the text
proof.text:
1. Read the sentences around the blank.
2. Find how many things are compared.
3. Find the clue words: **than**, **of all**, **ever**.

Point to the sentences that give the facts.

sentences.t: Today's storm is worse than yesterday's.
It is the worst storm of the year.

example.explain:
Today's storm is compared with **one** other storm, and we see **than** → **worse**.

Then it is compared with **every** storm of the year → **the worst**.

together.passage: Our class grew bean plants in three cups. The plant in the dark cupboard grew badly. It was thin and pale. The plant by the door looked ___ than that one. It had some green leaves. The plant on the sunny window was the best of all.
together.hint: Two plants are compared (than). Did the plant by the door do better or worse than the thin, pale one?
together.good: Yes! It had green leaves, and the cupboard plant was thin and pale, so it looked better.

sentences: Our class grew bean plants in three cups.
The plant in the dark cupboard grew badly.
It was thin and pale.
The plant by the door looked ___ than that one.
It had some green leaves.
The plant on the sunny window was the best of all.
evidence.stem: The answer was: better. Tap 2 sentences that prove the plant by the door did better than the cupboard plant.
evidence.wrong: This sentence does not compare the plant by the door with the cupboard plant. Look for what each plant looked like.

checks.passage: The traffic today is ___ than it was yesterday.
checks.why: Two days are compared, with than, so we use worse.

checks.passage: That was the ___ meal I have ever eaten. Everything was burnt!
checks.why: The meal is compared with every meal ever eaten, so it is the worst.

checks.passage: Huda reads more books than anyone. She is the ___ reader in our class.
checks.why: Huda is compared with the whole class, so she is the best reader.

again.title: Than or the?
again.text:
See **than**? Use better or worse.

See **the** ... **of all** or **ever**? Use best or worst.
again.example:
My cold is ___ than last week.

The clue is **than**, so: My cold is **worse than** last week.

slides.title: Well and badly compare too
slides.text:
**well → better → best**
**badly → worse → worst**

He sings **well**. She sings **better**. Their teacher sings **best**.

slides.title: Do not double up
slides.text:
Better, best, worse and worst already compare. Do not add more, most or -er.

✗ more better ✗ most worst ✗ worser
✓ better ✓ worst

slides.title: Same word, two jobs
slides.text:
**Better** can be an adjective: a **better** plan.

It can also be an adverb: She plans **better** now.

The form is the same. Look at what it describes.

proof.title: Prove it from the text
proof.text:
1. Find what is being compared: two times, two people, or a whole group.
2. Point to the facts in the text that show which one did more or less well.
3. Choose the form those facts prove.

sentences.t: Their uncle plays best of all.

example.explain:
**Well** describes how Turki plays. His cousin is compared with Turki → **better**.

Their uncle is compared with everyone → **best**.

together.passage: Our school held a spelling bee last month. In the first round, Majed spelled badly because he was nervous. He missed four words, including "surprise." In the second round, he did ___. He missed only two words. By the final round, Majed had calmed down. His teacher said it was his best effort of the year.
together.hint: Compare the two rounds. Did Majed miss more words or fewer words in the second round?
together.good: Yes! He missed two words instead of four, so he did better.

sentences: Our school held a spelling bee last month.
In the first round, Majed spelled badly because he was nervous.
He missed four words, including "surprise."
In the second round, he did ___.
He missed only two words.
By the final round, Majed had calmed down.
His teacher said it was his best effort of the year.
evidence.stem: The answer was: better. Tap 2 sentences that prove Majed did better in the second round.
evidence.wrong: This sentence does not tell how many words Majed missed. Find the numbers for each round.

checks.passage: Our team played most better after the break.
options: Our team played more well after the break.
Our team played better after the break.
Our team played gooder after the break.
Our team played more better after the break.
checks.why: Better already compares, so we do not add most or more.

checks.passage: My cough was bad on Monday, but it was even ___ on Tuesday.
checks.why: Two days are compared, and even needs a comparing word, so we use worse.

checks.passage: Four students read the poem aloud.
checks.stem: Which sentence correctly compares how they read?
options: Laila read best of all four.
Laila read more well than Dana.
checks.why: Best compares one reader with the whole group, and it needs no extra word.

again.title: Already done
again.text:
Better, best, worse and worst are **already** comparing words.

Use them **alone**. Do not add more, most, -er or -est.
again.example:
✗ This road is more worse.
✓ This road is **worse**.

Worse already means "more bad".

slides.title: Comparing in real writing
slides.text:
Writers use better, best, worse and worst to **judge**: the **best** solution, a **worse** result.

The form tells the reader how many things are being compared.

slides.title: Make it stronger
slides.text:
Put **much**, **far**, **even** or **a lot** before better or worse: **far better**, **much worse**.

Never use **more**: ✗ more better.

slides.title: Two choices, careful style
slides.text:
In careful writing, when there are only **two**, use **better** or **worse**: Of the two plans, this one is **the better**.

With three or more, use **the best** or **the worst**.

proof.title: Prove it from the text
proof.text:
1. Count the things compared. Look for **two**, **three**, **of the two**, **of all**.
2. Find the facts that show which one did more or less well.
3. Point to the sentences with the number and the result.

The form must match both.

sentences.t: The council looked at two ways to reduce traffic.
A new bus line would cost less than a wider road.
Of the two plans, the bus line was clearly the better choice.

example.explain:
There are only **two** plans, so careful writers use **the better**, not the best.

The second sentence gives the reason: it costs less.

together.passage: Last summer, our classroom was the hottest room in the school. The students tested three ways to keep it cool. First, they kept the door open, but hot air from the corridor made the room even worse. Next, they hung thick curtains on the sunny windows, and the room felt slightly cooler. Finally, they used the curtains and switched on the ceiling fans at the same time. This time the room felt much cooler than ever before. In their report, the students wrote that the third method worked ___ of the three.
together.hint: How many methods were tested? Which form do we use for three or more?
together.good: Yes! Three methods were compared, and the third made the room much cooler than ever, so it worked best.

sentences: Last summer, our classroom was the hottest room in the school.
The students tested three ways to keep it cool.
First, they kept the door open, but hot air from the corridor made the room even worse.
Next, they hung thick curtains on the sunny windows, and the room felt slightly cooler.
Finally, they used the curtains and switched on the ceiling fans at the same time.
This time the room felt much cooler than ever before.
In their report, the students wrote that the third method worked ___ of the three.
evidence.stem: The answer was: best. Tap 2 sentences that prove it: how many methods there were, and how well the third one worked.
evidence.wrong: This sentence describes one of the other methods. Find how many were tested and how the last one worked.

checks.passage: This year's harvest was far more better than last year's.
options: This year's harvest was far best than last year's.
This year's harvest was far more good than last year's.
This year's harvest was far gooder than last year's.
This year's harvest was far better than last year's.
checks.why: Far makes the comparison stronger. Better already compares, so more must go.

checks.passage: Of the two routes to the beach, the coast road is the ___ one because it has less traffic.
checks.stem: In careful writing, which word fits the blank?
checks.why: Only two routes are compared, and less traffic is a good thing, so careful writers use the better.

checks.passage: The storm damaged many houses, but the flood that followed caused even ___ damage.
checks.why: The flood is compared with the storm (two events), and even needs a comparing form: worse.

again.title: Count, then choose
again.text:
1. Count the things.
2. **Two** → better or worse (often with than).
3. **Three or more** → the best or the worst.
4. Never add more, most, -er or -est.
again.example: We tried three recipes. The second was **better** than the first, but the third was **the best** of all.
